title: Large Potential for CH4 Mitigation and Yield Improvement in China's Paddies Through Locally Optimized N Management
content:
Optimized nitrogen management in rice paddies simultaneously reduces methane emissions and increases yields. This study demonstrates that site-specific practices—including delayed fertilization, reduced nitrogen input, and deep placement—curtail methanogenesis by lowering soil nitrogen availability and organic matter decomposition. Integrating multiregional field experiments with machine learning, our analysis predicts that implementing these strategies across China's rice-growing regions could reduce methane emissions by 16% while increasing yields by 7%. These findings reveal an opportunity to achieve dual benefits for climate mitigation and food security, and provide an empirical basis for refining greenhouse gas emission inventories under diverse agricultural management regimes.


ABSTRACT

Nitrogen (N) management is critical for ensuring food security and mitigating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In rice paddies, the effectiveness of N management in maximizing yields and minimizing N losses is highly dependent on local environmental conditions and thus varies widely across regions. However, the influence of optimized, site-specific N management on methane (CH4) emissions remains poorly quantified and is not reflected in current IPCC Tier 1 methodologies. Here, we synthesize data from multiregional field experiments and conduct a meta-analysis to show that locally optimized N management practices—such as delayed fertilizer application, reduced N input, and deep placement—reduce CH4 emissions from rice paddies by 16%–21%. The experiments further show that these practices suppress CH4 emissions by lowering soil N availability and organic matter decomposition, thereby limiting substrates for methanogenesis. Combining survey data from 155 counties with machine learning models, we estimate that implementing optimized N strategies across China's rice-growing regions could reduce CH4 emissions by 16% while simultaneously increasing rice yields by 7%. These findings underscore the dual benefits of locally optimized N management for agricultural productivity and climate change mitigation, and provide a foundation for improving CH4 emission estimates under diverse management regimes.
